nodes.name: Tactical camera
nodes.purpose: Builds the battlefield camera from a pitch, a yaw, a zoom and a focus point, keeps it above the terrain it flies over, and shakes it for explosions.

nodes.name: Locomotor movement
nodes.purpose: Turns a destination into motive force for each movement style: tracked, wheeled, walking, climbing, hovering, winged and thrust-driven.

nodes.name: Rigid body physics
nodes.purpose: Integrates gravity, friction and motive force into velocity and position once per logic frame, then reconciles the body with the ground through contact, bounce and fall damage.

nodes.name: Object collision
nodes.purpose: Spatial partnership grid that answers distance and overlap questions, plus the push-apart response between two moving bodies.

nodes.name: Pathfinding
nodes.purpose: Grid search over the passable map with zone blockers, a sorted open list, turn-aware costs and a frame budget, followed by line-of-sight straightening.

nodes.name: Weapons and turrets
nodes.purpose: Turret yaw and pitch slew, elevation and arc tests before a shot, and the per-shot scatter applied to inaccurate weapons.

nodes.name: Projectile flight
nodes.purpose: Precomputed Bezier arcs that lift shells and rockets over intervening terrain and advance them along the curve at a fixed speed.

nodes.name: Terrain surface
nodes.purpose: Stores heights in a height map, interpolates a standing surface across two triangles per square, resolves bridge layers, and edits heights when explosions crater the ground.

nodes.name: Build placement
nodes.purpose: Legalises a structure site by rejecting bridges and by sampling the footprint height spread until the ground is flat enough to build on.

nodes.name: Group movement
nodes.purpose: Moves a selection as one body: picks the slowest healthy member pace, finds the group centre and leader, and leashes members to a bounded offset.

cards.name: Camera boom from pitch, yaw and zoom
cards.summary: The camera hangs off its focus point on a boom whose three legs come from a pitch, a yaw and a height, all scaled by zoom, so turning or zooming moves the eye without moving the target.
cards.behavior: A view keeps a pitch, a yaw, a zoom and a focus position. The boom is built trigonometrically: the vertical leg is the configured camera height, the leg pointing backwards along the view axis is that height divided by the tangent of the pitch, and the sideways leg is the backwards leg multiplied by the tangent of the yaw. Each update the eye is rebuilt from those legs scaled by the current zoom, then rotated about the horizontal axis by the pitch and about the up axis by the yaw, and finally translated to the focus point. Because zoom only scales the same three legs, zooming out keeps the look angle identical and simply recedes along the cone. A ground level offset is added to both eye and target so the whole construction can sit above a raised battlefield.

constants.name: Default vertical field of view
constants.unit: degrees of vertical field of view; static camera setting, no timestep

constants.name: Maximum zoom multiplier
constants.unit: multiple of the base boom length; static limit, no timestep

constants.name: Minimum zoom multiplier
constants.unit: multiple of the base boom length; static limit, no timestep

cards.name: Pitch clamp and field-of-view zoom
cards.summary: Pitch is held inside a shallow band, and the alternate real-zoom mode narrows the field of view with the square of the zoom while dropping the eye toward the ground.
cards.behavior: Every pitch request is clamped to one fifth of pi either side of level, so the camera can never look straight down or straight up, which keeps the skyline and the horizon stable while the player rotates. In the default mode the field of view is fixed and zoom only slides the eye along its boom. In the alternate real-zoom mode the boom stays at its neutral length, the zoom is clamped to the band between a half and one, the vertical field of view is multiplied by the square of that clamped value, the eye height is reduced toward the ground, and a pitch factor built as a quarter plus three quarters of the clamped zoom is applied along the view axis. The squared field-of-view term is what makes the last part of a zoom-in feel like a lens rather than a dolly.

constants.name: Pitch clamp divisor of pi
constants.unit: pi radians divided into the clamp, giving 36 degrees each way; static limit, no timestep

constants.name: Narrowest zoom scale for the field of view
constants.unit: fraction of neutral zoom at which the real-zoom field of view bottoms out; static clamp, no timestep

constants.name: Eye height share at minimum zoom
constants.unit: fraction of the eye height retained when the zoom is fully in; per rendered frame, rate unverified

constants.name: Fixed share of the pitch factor
constants.unit: fraction of the pitch factor fixed at one quarter, with the rest following the clamped zoom; per rendered frame, rate unverified

cards.name: Camera height follows the ground
cards.summary: The camera rides a chosen height above the highest of five nearby ground samples and eases back to that height once the player stops scrolling.
cards.behavior: Before each update the camera samples terrain height at its focus point and at four points offset by a fixed distance, keeping the largest of the five so that a hill just beside the view cannot swallow the eye. The requested height above ground is converted into a zoom by dividing by the vertical leg of the boom. While the player scrolls, the zoom only moves when the scroll magnitude is small or when the eye has fallen below the minimum or climbed above the maximum height above ground; at rest it eases toward the requested height by a fixed fraction each update. Scripted camera moves reset the target height to whatever the script produced, so a cinematic is not dragged back to the player height.

constants.name: Terrain probe offset
constants.unit: world units from the camera focus for each of the four extra ground samples; per camera update, rate unverified

constants.name: Camera height easing fraction
constants.unit: fraction of the remaining height error removed per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Minimum camera height above ground
constants.unit: world units; compiled default, static limit, no timestep

constants.name: Maximum camera height above ground
constants.unit: world units; compiled default, static limit, no timestep

cards.name: Distance-weighted camera shake
cards.summary: An explosion near the eye adds intensity that decays geometrically while flipping direction, and a second shaker layer adds damped sinusoidal rotations.
cards.behavior: A shake request names an epicentre and a severity. The horizontal distance from epicentre to eye is compared with a maximum range; beyond it nothing happens, inside it the severity intensity is scaled by one minus the normalised distance, added to the running intensity and capped. Each update the look-at point is displaced from its focus by the intensity along a random direction, the intensity is multiplied by a damping coefficient below one, and the direction sign flips so the whole view oscillates about the focus until the intensity falls under a small threshold. A separate shaker system keeps a list of shakers with a radius, a duration and a power: each one adds per-axis sinusoidal rotations whose start frequency is randomised between twelve and a half and fifteen turns per second and decays toward one turn per second, weighted unevenly so the camera pitches far more than it yaws, faded by distance and by remaining time, and finally clamped so the camera cannot roll over.

constants.name: Subtle shake intensity
constants.unit: world units of eye offset; compiled default, applied per update at 30 Hz until damped

constants.name: Strong shake intensity
constants.unit: world units of eye offset; compiled default, applied per update at 30 Hz until damped

constants.name: Shake range cutoff
constants.unit: world units from the epicentre; compiled default, static falloff radius, no timestep

constants.name: Oscillation damping per update
constants.unit: fraction of the offset intensity retained per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Shake intensity cap
constants.unit: world units of eye offset; static cap, no timestep

constants.name: Slowest shaker frequency
constants.unit: revolutions per second before conversion to radians; per shaker step of one thirtieth of a second

constants.name: Fastest shaker frequency
constants.unit: revolutions per second before conversion to radians; per shaker step of one thirtieth of a second

cards.name: Tracked steering and turn braking
cards.summary: A tank turns first and throttles by the angle left, creeps when it is nearly on target, and brakes harder as its stopping distance approaches.
cards.behavior: A tracked unit first turns toward its goal at its turn rate and keeps the remaining angle. That angle is divided by a quarter turn and clamped to one, and the goal speed becomes the desired speed scaled by one minus the coefficient, so a tank pointing away from its target barely moves while it pivots. When it is within two grid cells and still off by a small fraction of a quarter turn, the goal speed is further reduced to a share of its current speed, which stops tanks from orbiting the last waypoint. As the remaining distance along its path shrinks under the computed slow-down distance, the unit enters a braking state, seeds a braking factor just above one, and then scales the brake force by the square of the ratio between stopping distance and remaining distance, capped at a ceiling. Whatever the mode, the difference between goal and actual speed is turned into a motive force along the unit facing and clipped so it never exceeds the force needed to reach the goal speed.

constants.name: Turn angle divisor of pi
constants.unit: pi radians divided by this value, giving a 45 degree full-throttle cone; per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Precision creep angle threshold
constants.unit: fraction of a quarter turn of heading error above which the creep speed applies; per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Precision creep share
constants.unit: fraction of current speed used inside a two-cell approach; per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Braking factor on entering the brake
constants.unit: multiplier on braking force; per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Braking factor ceiling
constants.unit: upper bound on the squared braking multiplier; dimensionless per update at 30 Hz

cards.name: Stopping distance from speed over braking
cards.summary: The shared stopping helper squares the speed difference, divides by braking acceleration, halves it and adds a small fudge so units settle instead of creeping.
cards.behavior: The stopping helper subtracts the desired speed from the current speed and returns zero when the unit is already slow enough. Otherwise it divides the square of that difference by the magnitude of the maximum braking acceleration, halves the result, and multiplies by a fudge slightly above one. That is the constant-deceleration stopping distance with a margin, and it is the reason a unit begins to brake exactly early enough to arrive at its destination rather than overshoot. Tracked movement builds its own trigger distance by dividing the current speed by a closing factor and multiplying by the time to stop, and uses that distance to decide when to set the brake flag. Walking units instead substitute their template minimum speed once they cross the stopping distance, so infantry keep stepping instead of freezing on approach.

constants.name: Stopping distance halving factor
constants.unit: share of squared speed over braking acceleration; world units; per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Stopping distance fudge
constants.unit: multiplier on the computed stopping distance; dimensionless; per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Tracked closing factor
constants.unit: divisor on current speed when building the braking trigger distance; per update at 30 Hz

cards.name: Infantry weave and turn slowdown
cards.summary: Walking units drift left and right inside a bounded cone while following a path, and lose speed in proportion to the heading error they still have to correct.
cards.behavior: Walking movement computes the heading straight at the next path point and, if the locomotor has a wander factor, adds an offset that grows and shrinks with distance travelled. The offset is bounded by one eighth of a turn times that factor and reverses direction at each bound, so the unit weaves around its line rather than tracking it exactly. The resulting heading error is normalised, divided by a quarter turn and clamped to one, and the goal speed is the desired speed scaled by one minus that value, which is why a walking unit slows in a turn. Inside the stopping distance the goal speed becomes the locomotor minimum speed instead of zero, which keeps the walk cycle running as the unit arrives. The acceleration force is then clipped so it never exceeds what is needed for the speed change.

constants.name: Wander cone divisor of pi
constants.unit: pi radians divided by this value times the wander factor, giving a 22.5 degree half cone at factor one; per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Turn angle divisor of pi
constants.unit: pi radians divided by this value, normalising the heading error; per update at 30 Hz

cards.name: Altitude keeping by lift
cards.summary: Flying units hold a chosen height by solving the acceleration that closes the height error in one update, then clamping it to the lift the unit can produce.
cards.behavior: Vertical behaviour is chosen per locomotor: ignore height entirely, sit at sea level, hold a fixed absolute height, hold a height above the surface, hold a height above the highest bridge layer, or track the goal height exactly. In the relative modes the surface height is sampled under the unit, the preferred height is damped toward, and the error is converted into acceleration by assuming the correction completes in one update, which gives twice the height error minus the current vertical speed. That acceleration becomes lift after subtracting gravity, is clamped to the gross lift the unit can produce, and in the accurate mode is allowed three times that lift either way so a jet can finish a short landing. Descent braking is limited by net lift and climbing braking by gravity, and a separate vertical speed limit caps how quickly the unit may change altitude.

constants.name: Height correction gain
constants.unit: doubling factor turning height error minus vertical speed into acceleration; world units per frame squared at 30 Hz

constants.name: Accurate-mode lift ceiling
constants.unit: multiple of gross lift allowed when the accurate flag is set; dimensionless; per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Gravity
constants.unit: world units per frame squared at 30 Hz, negative downward; compiled default

cards.name: Euler integration with ground friction
cards.summary: Each logic frame accumulates gravity and friction into acceleration, folds acceleration into velocity and velocity into position, and zeroes velocities that are nearly still.
cards.behavior: The physics update is an explicit Euler step. Each update begins by clearing the accumulated acceleration, then adds gravity to the vertical component and applies friction. A grounded object gets a lateral drag along the axis perpendicular to its facing and, unless it is self-propelled that frame, a forward drag along its facing, both proportional to mass and to the matching velocity component. An airborne object gets drag proportional to velocity in all three axes instead. The accumulated acceleration is added to velocity, any component smaller than a small threshold is snapped to zero so units come to a clean rest, and the velocity is added to the transform translation. A braking unit may still change height but not its ground position. Rotation is integrated the same way from stored yaw, pitch and roll rates with a damping factor.

constants.name: Default forward friction
constants.unit: drag coefficient per update at 30 Hz, applied to forward velocity when not self-propelled

constants.name: Default lateral friction
constants.unit: drag coefficient per update at 30 Hz, applied to sideways velocity

constants.name: Default vertical friction
constants.unit: drag coefficient per update at 30 Hz, applied to vertical motion

constants.name: Maximum friction coefficient
constants.unit: upper clamp on a friction coefficient; dimensionless; static limit, no timestep

constants.name: Velocity zeroing threshold
constants.unit: world units per frame at 30 Hz; smaller velocity components are snapped to zero

cards.name: Ground contact, bounce and fall damage
cards.summary: The terrain surface is a hard floor with optional bounce, and a landing that is both hard and steep enough converts excess speed into damage.
cards.behavior: After integration the layer height under the object is sampled. If the new height is at or below it, the excess is removed from vertical velocity and the object is snapped onto the surface, which also clears its falling flag. A bouncy object instead receives an upward impulse proportional to its downward speed times a stiffness clamped between a hundredth and almost one, its rotation rates are damped, and its roll is levelled so it does not keep tumbling. When an object that was airborne one frame earlier touches down, the landing is judged: if the downward speed exceeds the template minimum fall speed, the object takes damage proportional to that excess, its mass and a damage factor, but only when the descent is steeper than roughly seventy-one degrees, tested by comparing vertical with horizontal speed. That angular test is what stops a unit from damaging itself while running down a gentle slope.

constants.name: Ground stiffness default
constants.unit: share of downward speed returned as bounce acceleration; compiled default; per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Bounce stiffness floor
constants.unit: lower clamp on bounce stiffness; dimensionless; static limit, no timestep

constants.name: Bounce stiffness ceiling
constants.unit: upper clamp on bounce stiffness; dimensionless; static limit, no timestep

constants.name: Bounce rotation damping
constants.unit: fraction of rotation rates kept on impact; per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Steep fall tangent
constants.unit: ratio of vertical to horizontal speed, about 71 degrees, required before a landing does damage; per landing, no timestep

cards.name: Sphere and circle collision separation
cards.summary: Airborne objects are compared as spheres, grounded objects as circles, and overlapping hulls push each other apart with a capped force along the line of centres.
cards.behavior: On a collision the physics handler first lets projectile modules claim the hit, then ignores containers, objects that are both parachuting, objects ignored by the AI obstacle test, and pairs that are deliberately allowed to overlap. Otherwise it measures centre to centre: an object above terrain uses full three-dimensional centres and bounding-sphere radii, while a grounded object uses only the horizontal plane and its bounding circle, so height differences are irrelevant on the ground. If the distance is larger than the sum of the radii nothing more happens. Otherwise the overlap is the sum minus the distance, capped at five world units for movable targets, and applied as a restoring force along the line of centres, with the separation distance floored at one unit so coincident objects cannot produce an unbounded force. Against immobile geometry the force instead comes from the mover speed, its mass and a stiffness, and its velocity is zeroed so it does not ricochet.

constants.name: Minimum separation for the force divisor
constants.unit: world units of centre distance; per collision, no timestep

constants.name: Maximum overlap correction
constants.unit: world units of push-apart overlap per collision at 30 Hz

constants.name: Minimum bounce speed divisor
constants.unit: logic frames per second divided by this value, giving about 0.0067 world units per frame at 30 Hz

cards.name: Octile grid search with a frame budget
cards.summary: Ground pathing is grid A* on ten-unit cells with straight and diagonal step costs, turn penalties, and a fixed number of cells searched each frame.
cards.behavior: The map is divided into cells ten world units on a side, each carrying terrain type, obstacle flags and a zone number, with bridges as separate layers. A search starts at the cell containing the unit, expands its eight neighbours, and keeps an open list sorted by estimated total cost. A straight step costs ten and a diagonal fourteen, an integer approximation of root two, and the remaining distance estimate charges one full step along the dominant axis plus half a step along the other, which keeps the estimate close to the octile path length without floating point. Additional penalties are charged for pinched cells and for direction changes, scaled by turn size: a forty-five degree turn costs four units, a right angle eight and a reversal sixteen. Searches are not finished in a single frame: the queue drains until the number of expanded cells reaches a fixed per-frame budget, which keeps a large battle responsive when many units repath at once.

constants.name: Path grid cell size
constants.unit: world units per cell edge; static map scale, no timestep

constants.name: Straight step cost
constants.unit: cost units per orthogonal step, one cell diameter; per search step, no timestep

constants.name: Diagonal step cost
constants.unit: cost units per diagonal step, approximating root two times the straight cost; per search step, no timestep

constants.name: Cells searched per frame
constants.unit: grid cells expanded per logic frame at 30 Hz

constants.name: Path request queue length
constants.unit: pending requests in the ring buffer; static size, no timestep

cards.name: Path straightening by line of sight
cards.summary: Grid paths are collapsed into straight runs by looking ahead for the farthest node the unit can reach in a straight line, keeping a few steps around layer changes.
cards.behavior: After a search returns a chain of cell centres the optimiser simplifies it. Starting from an anchor node it looks ahead for the farthest later node that the unit can walk to directly, given its permitted surfaces, its layer and the obstacle grid, and reconnects the anchor straight to it so the intermediate cells disappear. Around changes of layer, such as a unit stepping onto or off a bridge, it keeps up to three steps on each side and inserts a waypoint at the transition instead of cutting the corner, which is what prevents units from walking off a bridge deck. The scan also stops early at nodes that are marked non-optimisable, so sharp obstacle corners survive. Finally, single-cell orthogonal or diagonal steps between adjacent nodes are accepted as passable without a line test, so short staircase segments are not preserved as needless waypoints.

constants.name: Bridge transition steps kept
constants.unit: grid steps preserved on each side of a layer change; static limit, no timestep

constants.name: Single step span
constants.unit: world units, one grid cell, the step length accepted without a line test; per path node, no timestep

cards.name: Turret slew and snap
cards.summary: A turret advances toward its target at a fixed angular step and snaps exactly onto it once the remaining error is smaller than one step, yaw and pitch separately.
cards.behavior: A turret stores a yaw angle and, when the model supports it, a pitch angle. Each update it normalises the difference between the wanted and the current yaw. If that difference is smaller than this update turn rate it snaps exactly to the target and clears the rotating model state; otherwise it advances by exactly the turn rate toward the target and sets the rotating state, which drives the sound and animation. The pitch pass repeats the same procedure with its own rate and is skipped entirely for turrets that cannot pitch. Both rates are multiplied by per-call modifiers, which is how a slow heavy turret or a damaged one loses tracking, and a relative threshold flags when the barrel counts as aligned enough to fire. Both rates default to one hundredth of a radian per update, so a turret at the default rate needs a little over five seconds to sweep a quarter turn.

constants.name: Default turret turn rate
constants.unit: radians per update at 30 Hz, about 0.3 radians per second

constants.name: Default turret pitch rate
constants.unit: radians per update at 30 Hz

cards.name: Per-shot scatter in a ground disc
cards.summary: Inaccurate weapons stop aiming at the target point and shoot at a random point inside a disc instead, with a wider disc against infantry, and the scattered point is snapped down onto the ground layer.
cards.behavior: When a weapon carries a nonzero scatter radius, or carries an infantry inaccuracy value and the victim is infantry, firing stops aiming at the object and aims at a point instead. The effective radius is the weapon scatter plus, for infantry victims, the inaccuracy value. A radius is then drawn uniformly between zero and that sum, so some shots are nearly perfect, and an angle is drawn uniformly over a full turn; the two produce an offset in the horizontal plane only, keeping the shot position inside a disc around the target. For structures the horizontal aim point is taken from the centre of the bounding volume rather than the object origin, so a tall building is still covered by the disc. After the offset is applied the height is overwritten with the layer height at the scattered point, which forces a scattering shot to land on the ground or on the bridge deck the target stands on instead of flying at the centre height of the target.

constants.name: Scatter angle span in pi
constants.unit: radians as a multiple of pi, one full turn, drawn per shot; no timestep

constants.name: Minimum drawn radius
constants.unit: world units, lower bound of the random scatter radius; per shot, no timestep

cards.name: Elevation arc gate before firing
cards.summary: A weapon with a limited elevation refuses a shot whose target sits outside its vertical arc, unless the height difference is negligible.
cards.behavior: Before a shot is allowed the weapon checks the vertical geometry. Contact weapons and weapons without a pitch limit always pass. Otherwise the height difference between shooter and victim is compared with a small tolerance; inside that tolerance the shot is always allowed, because a tiny vertical offset cannot matter at range. Beyond it the shooter geometry is used to compute the range of pitches from the shooter to the target bounding volume, and the shot is allowed only when that pitch interval overlaps the weapon minimum and maximum target pitch. The consequence is visible on the battlefield: a flat-trajectory gun cannot hit a unit standing directly on the cliff above it, but can still hit the cliff face below and the ground in front. Keeping the interval test, rather than a single centre pitch, is what lets large targets be hit across the edges of the arc.

constants.name: Height tolerance for the arc test
constants.unit: world units of vertical difference; static test, no timestep

cards.name: Bezier shell arc over terrain
cards.summary: Shells and rockets fly a precomputed cubic Bezier whose two interior control points are lifted above the highest terrain between shooter and target.
cards.behavior: When a dumb projectile launches, its start is the barrel position and its end is the centre of the target. The flight path is a cubic Bezier with four control points. The two interior points lie on the straight line between the ends, at fractions of that distance taken from the projectile data, and their heights are the highest terrain found along the line plus the projectile own first and second heights, never below the start or end height. That is what makes an artillery shell clear a ridge the shooter cannot see over. The curve is then sampled into as many points as the curve length divided by the projectile flight speed, so the projectile advances roughly one speed-unit per update along its arc. While in flight it may creep its end point toward a moving target by a capped amount per update and rebuild the curve, and its model is oriented along the difference between consecutive path points.

constants.name: Bezier control points
constants.unit: control points in the cubic curve; static geometry, no timestep

constants.name: Target chase threshold
constants.unit: squared world units of target movement below which the flight path is not rebuilt; per update at 30 Hz

cards.name: Two-triangle height map sampling
cards.summary: Ground height is interpolated inside the triangle that contains the query point, giving a continuous standing surface across a grid of ten-unit squares.
cards.behavior: The world height map stores one byte per grid point, spaced ten world units apart, and each stored level is scaled to a fraction of a world unit. A query converts the world position into grid space, keeps the integer cell and the fractional position inside it, and then decides which of the two triangles that split the square contains the point by comparing the two fractions. Inside each triangle the height is reconstructed linearly from the three corner samples, so the surface rises and falls across the square instead of stepping at the grid points. The same call can also return a surface normal derived from a ring of neighbouring samples, which is what lets models and decals lie flat on a slope. Queries outside the playable area return a clipped edge height rather than failing, so objects falling off the map still find ground.

constants.name: Height map cell size
constants.unit: world units per grid square; static map scale, no timestep

constants.name: Height levels per cell
constants.unit: height map units making up one cell of elevation, giving 0.625 world units per stored level; static scale, no timestep

cards.name: Structures level the ground they stand on
cards.summary: A new structure samples the ground under its footprint, averages the samples, presses the footprint down to that height and then snaps itself onto the levelled ground.
cards.behavior: When a structure object is created, before it is registered as an obstacle, the terrain under its footprint is levelled. For a box footprint the four corners are rotated by the structure orientation and their axis-aligned bounds converted into grid ranges; for a round footprint the grid points inside the radius are used. Each grid point inside the shape is tested against the footprint triangles or the circle, and every matching point contributes its current ground height to an average, with the sample count guarding against an empty result. The average is quantised back into stored height levels with a rounding offset, and then clamped so it can never exceed the height at the structure origin, because the height map write used here can lower ground but not raise it. Every matching point writes that height to itself and to its eight neighbours, which smooths the pad into a 3x3 block and removes stair-stepping at the edge of the footprint. The structure is then moved down or up to the new ground height at its origin.

constants.name: Height quantisation rounding offset
constants.unit: stored height levels added before truncation when averaging world height into the height map; per footprint sample, no timestep

constants.name: Height levels per cell
constants.unit: height map units making up one cell of elevation, giving 0.625 world units per stored level; static scale, no timestep

cards.name: Scripted blast crater deformation
cards.summary: A blast-crater object placed by a script lowers the stored terrain heights around it, deepest at the centre and fading to nothing at the radius, and becomes a permanent pathfinding obstacle.
cards.behavior: Some maps and mission scripts place a blast-crater object rather than relying on an explosion. When such an object is created it is given its position and orientation, the terrain beneath it is edited, and only then is it added to the pathfinding map so that later searches treat the crater footprint as blocked. The edit uses the object radius to derive a grid range, then walks every grid point inside the circle, measuring its distance to the centre. A matched point has its stored height reduced by the radius times one minus the normalised distance, so the middle of the crater is deepest and the rim is barely changed, and a floor of one stored level prevents the edit from cutting below the minimum the map allows. Small geometry is skipped entirely, so only objects big enough to matter reshape the ground. Because the terrain is the same map that movement, camera and path queries read, the crater is permanent for the rest of the match.

constants.name: Crater falloff share
constants.unit: fraction of the radius used as the depth scale, so depth is radius times one minus normalised distance; per crater, no timestep

constants.name: Minimum stored crater height
constants.unit: height map levels; static floor, no timestep

cards.name: Build site flatness check
cards.summary: A structure site is rejected on a bridge and rejected whenever the height spread sampled across its footprint is too large, checked first coarse and then fine.
cards.behavior: Placement applies geometry checks first and then terrain checks. If the requested point is not on the ground layer but on a bridge, the site is refused outright because bridges cannot carry arbitrary structures. Otherwise the game samples the structure footprint at three times the height map cell size for a fast pass, then again at full cell resolution. At each sample it reads the terrain height and tracks the highest and lowest values seen; after each pass it rejects the site when that spread exceeds the configured allowed height variation, so a building cannot straddle a ridge or a crater lip. The same sampling marks the footprint restricted if any sample lands on terrain that cannot be built on. Only when both resolutions pass is the location considered legal.

constants.name: Coarse footprint sampling step
constants.unit: multiplier on the height map cell size for the fast pass, giving 30 world unit spacing; static sampling, no timestep

cards.name: Group pace and formation leash
cards.summary: A group moves at its slowest undamaged member pace and each member is sent to its formation offset, clamped to a multiple of its own radius so stragglers rejoin.
cards.behavior: When a group is recomputed it averages member positions to find a centre and then scans its members for the lowest current locomotor speed, skipping immobile and carried units and only counting members whose damage state is still better than the movement-penalty threshold, so one wrecked tank does not slow the whole selection. Alongside that scan it tracks which member sits closest to the centre. On a move order each member destination is its stored formation offset from the centre, or its present offset when no formation is active, and that offset vector is clamped to six times the member own bounding circle radius. The clamp is the leash: a unit that has drifted far from the formation is pulled back toward the destination instead of being sent around a long detour, and a unit already near its post is placed almost exactly on it. The per-unit destination is then pathed normally.

constants.name: Formation leash multiple
constants.unit: multiplier on the member bounding circle radius; world units; static limit, no timestep
